1. The frames show a bar chart of US consumer prices (CPI-U) from 1947 to August 2006. It is labeled "illustrative" and "history, not a forecast." A line marks a "first check" level, which looks like a starting payment amount. The idea seems to be testing whether a fixed payment keeps up with rising prices over 25-year stretches.

2. In frame 1, a green marker sits at the left edge, at the start of the series. In frames 2 to 4 the bars appear to be shifted or cut off at the right, so the chart ends at a different point. A counter then appears: "25-year stretches: 0 of 655 kept up." Frames 4 to 6 look nearly the same, so the counter stays at 0 of 655.

3. The label suggests that in every one of the 655 historical 25-year windows, a payment fixed at its first-check amount did not keep up with prices. A level, non-inflation-adjusted payment would therefore buy less over time in all of those windows. I'm inferring this from the label, because the image doesn't define "kept up." The chart's bars also don't clearly match a rising price index. They rise and fall, so they may show something else, such as the purchasing power of the payment.

4. A viewer might take away that a fixed-payment annuity loses purchasing power, so they should consider an option that adjusts for inflation. The frames don't say this directly. The "history, not a forecast" note also warns against treating the past as a prediction.

5. The animation did not state that advice. It is my own conclusion, drawn from the "0 of 655 kept up" counter and from your setup about choosing between two payout options. The animation only shows the historical result.
